newsitem.title: USA: Booming home sales suggest temporary economic slowing.
newsitem.headline: Booming home sales suggest temporary economic slowing.

text.p: Surprisingly brisk May new-home sales, reported Monday by the Commerce Department, demonstrated the economy's durability as rising consumer incomes fostered a pickup in spending.

Coupled with separate regional reports of rising industrial activity, the data sent a chill through financial markets a day before Federal Reserve policy-makers start a two-day meeting on interest-rate policy.
Bond prices dropped sharply in the morning, sending long-term interest rates higher, while stock prices were down about 25 points on the New York Stock Exchange by noon before partly recovering.

Nonetheless, the Federal Open Market Committee was widely expected to keep rates steady when it announces its decision Wednesday afternoon, in the absence of clear signs of rising inflation and amid other signs that economic growth is cooling from its overheated first-quarter pace.

Sales of new homes rebounded by 7.1 percent in May to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 825,000 units -- well above forecasts and the strongest monthly pickup in six months -- after a revised 8.1 percent drop in April.
The supply of homes for sale on the market dropped to the lowest in nearly 26 years, just 4.1 months' worth at the rate that May sales were taking place.
Another Commerce Department report showed consumer spending increased by 0.3 percent in May to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $5.37 trillion after a slight 0.1 percent April rise.
Incomes from wages, salaries and all other sources were up an identical 0.3 percent in May to $6.77 trillion a year after a 0.2 percent pickup in April.

Rising incomes, powered by steady job growth, underline the vigour in the consumer sector that has sent confidence soaring, but it added to concern among some analysts that a second-quarter slowdown could prove temporary.
If so, that could bring higher interest rates later in the year to keep the economy from growing at a pace that the Fed might feel raised the risk of price inflation.

Economist David Seiders of the National Association of Home Builders said the slim supply of new homes for sale -- the lowest monthly supply since it also was at 4.1 months' worth in July 1971 -- showed "very taut" conditions in the face of strong demand.
"The real question now is 'Are we poised for a rebound in production in the second half with these inventory levels?'" Sieders said.
"We're betting against it," he added, and also counting on the Fed to hold interest rates steady this week.

Joel Naroff, a Philadelphia-based economist with First Union Corp. of Charlotte, N.C., said central bank policy-makers will be assessing a scenario in which housing appears likely to continue contributing significantly to an expanding economy rather than acting as a brake on national activity.

"FOMC members ... may be amazed at how wonderful conditions are, but they have to be concerned that there are no signs that the strong growth (in housing) will moderate during the second half of this year," Naroff said.

Chicago purchasing managers issued their own Chicagoland Business Barometer on Monday that showed a big pickup in activity in the industrial Midwest to 61.5 in June from 56.8 in May with production and orders up sharply. Any measure over 50 indicates a strengthening regional industrial economy

New York regional purchasing managers similarly reported their index of New York-area business conditions soared to 64.9 in June from 50.8 in May, further buttressing the impression of firm underlying economic activity.

New-home sales were especially strong during May in the Midwest, jumping 23.9 percent to 166,000. In the Northeast, sales rose 15.1 percent in May to 107,000 and in the South they were up 5.3 percent to 357,000.
The only region where sales fell during May was in the West, where they were down 4.4 percent to 195,000.
